chapter_theme: Farming is the world's first occupation because everyone, including kings and renouncers, ends up depending on it. Those who live by it alone owe nothing to anyone, and the land itself responds to attention, as a wife or a mocking woman would.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its excellence (1031), the excellence of those who do it (1032-1036), how it is done (1037-1039), and the fault of not doing it, which also leads into the following chapter on poverty (1040).

1031.reading: Though it whirls about, the world follows the plough; therefore, though toilsome, farming is foremost.
1031.nuance: The verse concedes the toil and doesn't romanticize it (உழந்தும்). Its case is a structural one: all other paths end up at the same place. சுழன்றும் may also suggest the world turning like a wheel behind the plough, and Kalaignar's version keeps this.

1032.reading: Those who plough are the linchpin of the world's people, for they carry all those who can't do it and rise to other things.
1032.nuance: Parimelazhagar says உழுவார் extends to those who have others plough for them, citing a parallel, which brings landowners into the honour. The verse doesn't say so. He reports a variant, தொழுவாரே, in which those unable to plough cringe to their patrons, which anticipates 1033.

1033.reading: Only those who live by eating from their own ploughing truly live; all others bow to eat, and walk behind.
1033.nuance: Parimelazhagar's வாழ்வார் are those who belong to themselves (தமக்குரியராய்): the verse is about independence as much as food.

positions.position: The rest bow to other patrons and live on what they are given.
positions.quote: பிறரைத் தொழுது, அவர் சில கொடுப்பத் தம் உயிரோம்பி

positions.position: The rest bow to the farmers themselves.

1034.reading: Those with the shade of grain-ears will see many umbrellas' shade under their own umbrella.
1034.nuance: The royal umbrella is set against the grain's shade. Manakkudavar notices a pun: an 'umbrella-less shade'. The verse claims that farming, not armies, underwrites conquest.

positions.position: The umbrella is that of their king, whose conquests their grain makes possible.
positions.quote: பலவேந்தர் - குடை நிழலதாய மண் முழுதினையும் தம் வேந்தர்குடைக்கீழே காண்பர்.

positions.position: Farmers themselves have the strength to bring all governments under them.

1035.reading: Those whose way is to eat what their hands produce don't ask, and give to those who ask without hiding.
1035.nuance: The hand is the verse's key: it labours and it gives, and it never stretches out. Parimelazhagar restricts கைசெய் to ploughing, while Kalaignar makes it any self-earned work. The verse anticipates the chapters on begging, whose word கரவாது it uses.

1036.reading: If farmers fold their hands, even those who say they have given up desire won't be able to stay in that state.
1036.nuance: என்பார், 'those who say', carries a slight edge. Parimelazhagar extends the verse to all of this world's aims, the next world's and liberation. He and another reading differ on whether விழைவது is food or desire in general.

1037.reading: If you dry the soil so that a measure of earth falls to a quarter, it will grow abundantly without even a handful of manure.
1037.nuance: A rare place where the Kural gives technical advice, with exact weights. Kalaignar reads the reduction as coming from repeated ploughing, while Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar have sun-drying. The moral of attention before input is left unstated.

1038.reading: Manuring is better than ploughing, and after weeding, guarding is better than watering.
1038.nuance: A ladder of care in which each stage beats the previous one, and watchfulness comes out above water, the thing plants most obviously need. Parimelazhagar sets out the sequence of five.

1039.reading: If the owner stays away and doesn't go, the land will resent and sulk like a wife.
1039.nuance: ஊடி is a term from love poetry, used here in farm advice. கிழவன், 'owner', also means husband, a double meaning that makes the comparison work. Parimelazhagar says that the owner must go himself and not send others, which is in some tension with his widening of உழுவார் in 1032.

1040.reading: Seeing those who say 'we have nothing' and sit idle, the good woman called Land laughs.
1040.nuance: The Earth doesn't scold but laughs. Parimelazhagar notes this is the bridge to the next chapter on poverty, and he has a variant இரப்பாரை, 'those who beg', which Manakkudavar uses, pointing to the later chapters too.

links.note: The same earth responds in two ways. In 151 it supports even those who dig into it, the model of patience. In 1040 it laughs at those who won't dig. Being dug is what it tolerates and even wants, so the virtue chapter's image becomes a joke on the idle.
'X என்னும் நல்லாள்' is a shared formula. Shame the good woman turns her back on the drunk, and Land the good woman laughs at the idle. Both personified women judge men.
ஊடல் is love's sweet sulk in 1330, delightful when embrace follows. 1039 borrows the word to warn an absent owner: the land, like a spouse, wants presence, and here the sulk costs him the harvest.
42 makes the householder the support of renouncers, and 1036 sets the farmer a level below, as the support of renouncing itself. The chain of dependence runs lower than the book of virtue showed.

1065 says even thin gruel earned by one's own effort is the sweetest thing. 1033 makes that a social claim: only those who eat from their own ploughing truly live. The chapters on begging supply this chapter's value.
1051 tells one to ask of those worth asking and makes refusal their fault, not yours. 1035 presents a person who never needs the permission, and who is on the giving end of that same act.

source_issues: 1032: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.
1034: Pope's gloss reads 'patriotic farmers desire to bring all other states under the control of their own king', adding a motive not found in the Tamil.
1036: Pope's gloss says 'ascetic state will fail', dropping the verse's என்பார்.
